author: high7
claim: Let \(p\) be a prime and let \(G\) be a finite group of order \(p^n\) for some integer \(n\ge 1\). Prove that the order of the center \(Z(G)\) is divisible by \(p\), and hence that \(Z(G)\) contains a nonidentity element.
evidence:
Let G act on itself by conjugation. For x in G, define
C_G(x)={g in G : gx=xg}. This is a subgroup: the identity belongs to it, and if a,b belong to C_G(x), then ab^{-1} also commutes with x. The map
gC_G(x) -> gxg^{-1}
from the left cosets of C_G(x) to the conjugacy class of x is well defined and bijective. Indeed, multiplying g on the right by an element commuting with x does not change gxg^{-1}; and two elements g_1,g_2 produce the same conjugate precisely when g_2^{-1}g_1 lies in C_G(x). Therefore the conjugacy class of x has size [G:C_G(x)].

The left cosets of C_G(x) partition G into equally sized sets, so
|G|=[G:C_G(x)] |C_G(x)|.
Because |G|=p^n and p is prime, both positive integer factors are powers of p. Thus [G:C_G(x)] is a power of p. Moreover, [G:C_G(x)]=1 exactly when C_G(x)=G, which is exactly when x lies in Z(G). Consequently every conjugacy class of a noncentral element has size divisible by p.

Conjugacy is an equivalence relation, so its classes partition G. The class of every element of Z(G) is a singleton. Choose one representative x_i from each conjugacy class contained in G\Z(G), with i ranging from 1 to r (allowing r=0). Counting the partition gives the class equation
|G|=|Z(G)|+sum_{i=1}^r [G:C_G(x_i)].
The left side is divisible by p because n>=1, and every term in the sum is divisible by p by the preceding paragraph. Hence |Z(G)| is divisible by p.

Finally, the identity element belongs to Z(G). Since a prime p satisfies p>=2 and |Z(G)| is a positive multiple of p, |Z(G)|>=2; therefore Z(G) contains an element different from the identity.

glossary.x_i: a representative of the i-th noncentral conjugacy class
glossary.r: the number of conjugacy classes contained in G minus Z(G)

author: high3
claim: Direct class-equation plan: solved; all subgoals yield the full theorem.
evidence: Let G act on itself by conjugation. For x∈G let C_G(x)={g∈G:gx=xg}. The map gC_G(x)↦gxg^{-1} is well-defined: replacing g by gc with c∈C_G(x) does not change gxg^{-1}. It is onto the conjugacy class, and equality gxg^{-1}=hxh^{-1} implies h^{-1}g∈C_G(x), hence gC_G(x)=hC_G(x); therefore it is one-to-one. Thus the conjugacy class of x has size [G:C_G(x)]. Lagrange's theorem gives |C_G(x)|∣p^n, so [G:C_G(x)] is a power of p. The class has size 1 exactly when x commutes with every element of G, i.e. x∈Z(G). Hence every noncentral class has size divisible by p. Since conjugacy classes partition G, |G|=|Z(G)|+Σ_i |K_i| over the noncentral classes K_i. Both |G|=p^n and every |K_i| are divisible by p, so p∣|Z(G)|. As Z(G) contains the identity and its positive order is a multiple of the prime p≥2, it has at least two elements and therefore contains a nonidentity element.

author: high6
claim: The full target theorem is solved directly by the class equation for the conjugation action.
evidence:
Let G act on its underlying set by conjugation: g sends x to gxg^{-1}. For x in G, define C_G(x)={g in G: gx=xg}. The map from the set of left cosets G/C_G(x) to the conjugacy class of x, given by gC_G(x) maps to gxg^{-1}, is well-defined and bijective. Indeed, replacing g by gc with c in C_G(x) does not change gxg^{-1}; conversely, gxg^{-1}=hxh^{-1} implies h^{-1}g commutes with x, so gC_G(x)=hC_G(x). Thus the conjugacy class of x has cardinality [G:C_G(x)].

The left cosets of C_G(x) partition G into equally sized sets, so |G|=[G:C_G(x)]|C_G(x)|. Since |G|=p^n, the positive divisor |C_G(x)| of p^n is p^m for some integer m with 0≤m≤n. If x is not in Z(G), then C_G(x) is a proper subgroup of G, hence m<n. Therefore its conjugacy class has size p^{n-m}, which is divisible by p.

The conjugacy classes partition G. The class of x is a singleton exactly when x lies in Z(G). Choosing one representative x_i from each noncentral conjugacy class gives
p^n=|G|=|Z(G)|+Σ_i [G:C_G(x_i)].
Every summand in the sum is divisible by p, and p divides p^n because n≥1. Hence p divides |Z(G)|. Finally, the identity belongs to Z(G), so |Z(G)| is positive. A positive integer divisible by the prime p is at least p≥2; therefore Z(G) has an element other than the identity.

author: high
claim: Let \(p\) be a prime and let \(G\) be a finite group of order \(p^n\) for some integer \(n\ge 1\). Prove that the order of the center \(Z(G)\) is divisible by \(p\), and hence that \(Z(G)\) contains a nonidentity element.
evidence:
Let G act on its underlying set by conjugation: for g,x in G, send x to gxg^{-1}. For x in G define
C_G(x)={g in G: gx=xg}
and
Cl_G(x)={gxg^{-1}:g in G}.
The set C_G(x) is a subgroup of G: it contains 1_G; if a,b commute with x then ab commutes with x; and if a commutes with x then a^{-1} commutes with x.

Define a map from the set of left cosets of C_G(x) to Cl_G(x) by
gC_G(x) maps to gxg^{-1}.
This map is well-defined and injective because, for g,h in G,
gC_G(x)=hC_G(x)
if and only if h^{-1}g belongs to C_G(x), which is equivalent to
h^{-1}gx=xh^{-1}g,
and this is equivalent to gxg^{-1}=hxh^{-1}.
It is surjective by the definition of Cl_G(x). Therefore
|Cl_G(x)|=[G:C_G(x)].

The left cosets of C_G(x) partition G into [G:C_G(x)] sets, each having |C_G(x)| elements. Hence
p^n=|G|=[G:C_G(x)]|C_G(x)|.
In particular, |C_G(x)| is a positive divisor of p^n. By unique factorization of positive integers, there is an integer m with 0<=m<=n such that |C_G(x)|=p^m. If x is not in Z(G), then some element of G does not commute with x, so C_G(x) is a proper subgroup of G. Thus |C_G(x)|<|G|, so m<n. Consequently
|Cl_G(x)|=[G:C_G(x)]=p^{n-m},
which is divisible by p.

The conjugacy classes partition G. Moreover, Cl_G(x) is the singleton {x} if and only if gxg^{-1}=x for every g in G, which holds if and only if x commutes with every element of G, that is, if and only if x belongs to Z(G). Choose one representative x_i from each noncentral conjugacy class, with i ranging from 1 to r, where r is a nonnegative integer (and the sum below is empty if r=0). The partition into central singleton classes and noncentral classes gives the class equation
|G|=|Z(G)|+sum_{i=1}^r |Cl_G(x_i)|.
Every summand in the sum is divisible by p, and |G|=p^n is divisible by p because n>=1. Therefore their difference |Z(G)| is divisible by p.

Finally, 1_G belongs to Z(G), so |Z(G)| is positive. A positive integer divisible by the prime p is at least p, and p>=2. Hence |Z(G)|>=2. Since one element of Z(G) is 1_G, Z(G) contains an element different from 1_G, namely a nonidentity element.
